summary: An official view of the IAB, coordinated with the Federal Networking Council, explaining the role of GOSIP, the U.S. government's OSI profile, in relation to the Internet. It is informational.

subtitle: Clarifying how the U.S. government's OSI profile relates to Internet evolution.

tldr.problem: As August 1990 approached when GOSIP became mandatory for U.S. government procurements, confusion spread about what the requirement meant for the Internet and existing networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC, endorsed by the IAB, FNC, and IETF, clarified that GOSIP is a procurement specification, not a mandate for immediate protocol transition, and that multi-protocol environments would persist.
tldr.outcome: It calmed fears about forced migration from TCP/IP to OSI and set expectations for gradual, responsible integration of OSI protocols into the Internet.

today: RFC 1169 is an informational RFC representing the official view of the IAB, FNC, and IETF on GOSIP's role. While GOSIP itself became less prominent after the 1990s, the document's principles proved sound: the Internet did integrate OSI protocols gradually and responsibly, TCP/IP remained dominant, and multi-protocol operation became standard practice rather than a temporary anomaly.

sections.title: The Context: GOSIP and Confusion
sections.content:
In 1990, there was widespread confusion about GOSIP (U.S. Government OSI Profile), a federal procurement standard that was to become mandatory in August 1990. The misunderstanding was serious: many believed GOSIP mandated an immediate, total transition to OSI protocols, abandoning TCP/IP entirely.

The roots lay in real technical change. The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) suite was an international standard for networking protocols, an alternative to the TCP/IP suite that powered the Internet. The U.S. government wanted standardized OSI products for procurement, so NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) created GOSIP as a procurement specification defining which OSI protocols the government would buy.

This RFC, endorsed by the Internet Activities Board (IAB), the Federal Networking Council (FNC), and the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), aimed to clarify GOSIP's actual scope and correct the widespread misunderstandings.
sections.eli5: The government decided to use new network technology, and people thought that meant everything would suddenly change to the new system. This paper explained what the government actually meant.

sections.title: What GOSIP Actually Is
sections.content:
GOSIP, published as Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 146, specifies which OSI protocols the U.S. government would procure and use. It was necessary because OSI standards contained many optional choices and configurations, some of which were incompatible. GOSIP refined the OSI standards through a process involving commercial vendors and users at the OSI Implementors Workshops (OIW), hosted four times yearly by NIST since 1983.

The GOSIP document had three parts: an announcement explaining objectives and applicability; technical specifications defining which OSI protocols to procure; and appendices describing plans for future OSI standards. GOSIP Version 1 was published in August 1988 and adopted as FIPS in February 1989, becoming a federal procurement requirement in August 1990. A second version was planned for 1990, becoming mandatory 18 months later.

The Federal Networking Council, the Internet Activities Board, and the IETF committed to "responsible integration of OSI" based on sound planning. This meant OSI would be added to the Internet without losing existing services, and a multi-protocol environment would exist for a prolonged period.
sections.eli5: GOSIP was a shopping list: here's what the government will buy when it needs new networking equipment. It wasn't a rule to throw out everything else.

sections.title: The Misunderstandings Clarified
sections.content:
The RFC addressed several widespread myths:

Not an immediate total transition. FIPS 146 is a procurement specification, not a protocol transition mandate. It says when the government acquires new network products, those products must support OSI where feasible and if the application requires OSI capabilities. It does not require existing installed equipment to be replaced.

Applies only to new procurement and major upgrades. GOSIP applies most readily to procurements of new networks and major upgrades. Adding a few compatible devices to an existing network does not trigger GOSIP compliance requirements.

Not exclusive. GOSIP is not exclusive: when agencies implement GOSIP, they may still procure and use other protocols. Agencies might retain TCP/IP, use protocol converters during transition, or take advantage of enhanced features in non-GOSIP protocols. GOSIP provides Government-wide interoperability but does not mandate abandoning all alternatives.

Waivers are possible. Waivers from GOSIP compliance are available when adherence would prevent an agency from accomplishing its mission or would cause adverse financial effects. Agency heads have authority to grant waivers. No waiver is needed if GOSIP does not apply to a procurement.

OSI is still incomplete. Many OSI protocols were still under development. GOSIP Versions 1 and 2 addressed only fully standardized OSI protocols. As new standards emerged for directory services, network management, and dynamic routing, GOSIP would be revised to incorporate them.
sections.eli5: GOSIP meant: when the government buys new equipment, make sure it understands OSI. But it didn't mean throw out TCP/IP or break existing networks.

sections.title: Roles of the IETF, Infrastructure Agencies, and Users
sections.content:
The RFC defined clear roles for different players in the integration process:

The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force), working under the IAB, would define the technical mechanisms for accommodating OSI in the Internet, enabling coexistence and interoperability between OSI and TCP/IP during multi-protocol operation. IETF activities included drafting RFCs, creating input to GOSIP, contributing to the GOSIP Users' Guide, and participating in the OSI Implementors Workshop. The IETF had a dedicated working area for OSI integration, with official representation on the GOSIP Advanced Requirements Group.

Federal agencies providing Internet infrastructure (NSF, NASA, DOE, DARPA) would support essential services: routing of ISO 8473 packets in backbones like NSFnet, application-level gateways enabling TCP/IP to OSI interoperability, and OSI directory services.

Federal agencies using Internet services should identify their requirements, participate in IETF and GOSIP groups, and plan OSI adoption within their networks based on technical and management realities. Each agency should develop its own policy on GOSIP adoption and begin planning for GOSIP-compliant products.
sections.eli5: Different organizations had different jobs: the technical groups (IETF) figured out how to make OSI and TCP/IP work together; big network operators set up the infrastructure; using agencies planned their own transitions.

sections.title: The Path Forward
sections.content:
The RFC summarized key principles for OSI integration. GOSIP as a procurement specification focused on what the government would buy, not how quickly systems would transition. Multi-protocol operation would continue for a considerable period as OSI products matured and standards were completed. Responsible planning, not crisis-driven migration, would guide integration.

The government had five key obligations: (1) GOSIP applies to procurement, not to existing equipment; (2) when GOSIP applies, it does not exclude other protocols; (3) when GOSIP applies, waivers are available for specific agency needs; (4) agencies bear responsibility for planning their OSI compliance and determining when GOSIP applies to particular procurements; and (5) NIST would support this integration through updated standards and the GOSIP Users' Guide.

This clarification was essential: it allowed the Internet community to plan responsibly for OSI coexistence rather than panic over a mandatory overnight switch that was never intended.
sections.eli5: The paper said: yes, OSI is coming, but not overnight. You can use both systems together. Plan carefully, and you'll do fine.
